new_statements.quote: Final Prominence (whatever its source) is confirmed in Saulteaux nouns (213) and verbs (214) both in isolation and within a sentence (215). Impressionistically, this prominence is marked by a rise in pitch and intensity. [...] In fact, there is no consistent acoustic evidence for either primary or secondary stress in Saulteaux regardless of the predictions above. Some syllables may sound more prominent, but their location is not predictable from item to item. [...] Perhaps Saulteaux Ojibwe is, in fact, a final stress language. new_statements.rule_in_words: The one consistent prominence is on the final syllable of every word (noun or verb, in isolation and in running speech), realized as a rise in pitch and intensity; Miller cannot decide whether this is final word stress or a boundary effect. The traditional description (Logan 2001:11 after Voorhis 1976 and Cote 1984, also in Cote 2012:15) is a quantity-sensitive alternating system: every long-vowel syllable is stressed, the last syllable is always stressed, and every second syllable in a run of short-vowel syllables is stressed, with the remaining short vowels reduced or elided; no primary stress is singled out. Miller, listening to 24 h of recordings from eight speakers, found no consistent primary or secondary stress matching either the traditional or Hayes' iambic predictions, and retains iambic feet only to account for optional weak-vowel syncope. If a single positional reading is required, fixed: final syllable is the only pattern both sources agree on; weight-sensitive (iambic) is the traditional rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Miller 2018: no consistent acoustic evidence for primary or secondary stress; left-to-right iambic foot structure still motivated by optional syncope of foot-weak short vowels (mostly pronominal clitics). Logan 2001:11: several stressed syllables per word (all long-vowel syllables plus every second short-vowel syllable), no primary/secondary distinction made.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Logan notes unstressed short vowels are elided far less than in eastern dialects (Odawa). Miller notes results are impressionistic and that an acoustic study is still needed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: nouns and verbs in citation form and inside sentences (Miller exx. 213-215). Miller's Table 5.1 places Final Prominence at the right edge of the whole verb complex (including the object-number clitic) and at the end of each root of a compound; Logan's rule is stated for 'every word'.
new_statements.identity_note: ojw / west1510 = Saulteaux (Plains or Western Ojibwe) of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Miller 2018's data are from eight Manitoba speakers born in Berens River, Roseau River, Gypsumville, Hollow Water, Sandy Bay and Duck Bay (Lake Winnipeg / Interlake area); Valentine's dialectology puts Berens River in a northern (Berens River/Northwestern, cf. ojb nort2961) group, but Miller labels the whole sample Saulteaux. Logan 2001 (the traditional rule) is based on speakers from the Cote and Muscowpetung reserves in Saskatchewan, squarely ojw. Tallman 2011 = Manitoba Saulteaux; Cote 2012 = Cote First Nation, Saskatchewan.

sources.note: Sec. 1.0 'Stress', p. 11 (PDF p. 25): 'The placement of stress in Ojibwa (including Saulteaux) can be satisfactorily explained in a fairly straightforward fashion and there can be several stressed syllables within a word. There are three basic rules for stress assignment (as put forward by Voorhis et al 1976 and Cote 1984): 1) Each syllable with a long vowel will be stressed. 2) The last syllable of every word is obligatorily stressed. 3) Every second syllable in a sequence of syllables with short vowels will be stressed. The other short vowels are realized in one of the unstressed allomorphs…

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pp. 14-15 (PDF 28-29): reproduces Valentine's (2001:54) metrical stress rules (weak-strong feet from the left; only short vowels weak; last vowel always strong) and says this 'is similar to Saulteaux stress assignment as described by Cote (1985) and Voorhis et al. (1976)', then restates the same three rules as Logan (long vowels stressed; last syllable obligatorily stressed; every second short-vowel syllable stressed, others reduced to [ə] or elided). Second-hand.

sources.citation: Valentine, J. Randolph. 1996. Phonological parameters of Ojibwe dialect variation. Papers of the 27th Algonquian Conference, 287-323.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'STRESS' pp. 312-314: pan-Ojibwe 'quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word.. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical'; in Berens River Ojibwe 'the correlate of stress in these dialects is pitch'. p. 288: Valentine (1987 MS) contains an instrumental analysis of stress and intonation in a Peguis, Manitoba (Saulteaux) text. Nothing Saulteaux-specific on stress placement.

sources.citation: Tallman, Adam J. R. 2011. Acoustic correlates of lenis and fortis stops in Manitoba Saulteaux. MA thesis, University of Manitoba.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Acoustic study of stops with six Manitoba speakers; no stress description of its own. Cites the literature that 'only short vowels undergo this reduction and that long vowels are always stressed (e.g. Piggott 1980, Valentine 2001, Swierzbin 2003)' and that short vowels are often lenited (Piggott 1980, Valentine 1994, 2001), using it to explain more preaspiration after short vowels.
